newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia releases parliamentary candidate list.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia releases parliamentary candidate list.

text.p: Indonesia's election commission on Friday announced a list of 2,293 approved candidates, screened by government and security agencies, for next May's general elections.
As expected, the list excludes ousted Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) leader Megawati Sukarnoputri, or her supporters, who are challenging their removal in the courts.
Interior Minister Yogie Memet said the list would be sent to every village and neighbourhood in the country so the public could comment on the candidates before February 18.

"It is not yet guaranteed that those on the list will become members of parliament as we are still waiting for the thoughts and concerns of the people, which will be checked for accuracy (and) which are very influential," said Memet, who also heads the elections commission, the General Elections Institute.

Megawati, whose removal sparked Jakarta's worst riots in years in July, sued Memet and the institute in September over the body's refusal to accept her supporters' list of candidates. Their refusal effectively shut her out of the election process.
The case is still before the courts.
The official campaign period runs from April 29 to May 23 with the polls on May 29.
Soetoyo, head of the commission's special research committee, said his group had struck off a number of candidates put forward by the three authorised parties.
Military and police intelligence bodies also take part in the screening process.

Only the ruling Golkar, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist PDI are allowed to contest elections run concurrently for municipal and regional legislatures as well as the national parliament.
The candidates announced on Thursday are for the 500-seat national parliament, of which 75 seats are directly appointed by the armed forces. Members of the military do not vote.
Candidates for municipal and regional legislatures go through a similar vetting process.

Soetoyo said the committee had found 257 proposed national candidates had not fulfilled all requirements. Anyone linked to the banned Indonesian Communist Party (PKI) or the failed 1965 coup blamed on the PKI is automatically barred.
Soetoyo said 130 proposed candidates from the PPP, 21 from Golkar and 106 from the PDI had failed the screening. He did not give any reasons.
Surjadi, the government-backed leader of the PDI, said his party would consider appealing against the rejection of its candidates once the election commission had given its reasons.
He said he expected an orderly election campaign despite a protest on Thursday by some 300 backers of his ousted rival Megawati.
PPP Secretary-General Tosari Widjaya told reporters his party might appeal the rejection of some of its nominees.
"We are considering taking our concerns to court," he said.

Widjaya said some candidates who were civil servants had been rejected after they did not receive permission to run from their superiors, while others failed to have their certificates of non-involvement with the PKI processed by police in time.
All civil servants are members of the Indonesia Civil Servants Corps, a member of Golkar, and there is continuing debate over whether they are obligated to vote for the ruling party.
Golkar won 68 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.
